feat.title: Feature Design
feat.subtitle: Three capability domains, nine core features
feat.c1.desc: 64-bit, k-ordered, globally unique; 4M+ per second per node, no central coordinator and no database round-trips.
feat.c2.desc: Timestamp / datacenter / worker / sequence widths are all adjustable; the default 5+5+12 supports 1024 nodes. Every bit borrowed shortens the lifespan — check with lifespan_ms() first.
feat.c3.desc: Turn a generated ID back into timestamp, datacenter, worker and sequence — for debugging and sharding. datetime is UTC, stable across machines.
feat.c4.desc: The sequence strategy is a trait: sequential, random and Redis ship built in; implement SequenceResolver to plug in your own without touching the core.
feat.c5.desc: A configurable tolerance window absorbs NTP jitter; beyond it clock_drift_strategy decides: wait spins until the clock catches up (within budget), throw refuses to generate.
feat.c6.desc: Eight opt-in adapters: axum, actix-web, rocket, poem, salvo, warp, bee-rust and e-cat. A handler declares a Guard parameter and generates IDs; a missing registration is a 500.
feat.c7.desc: Two entry points — builder and environment — validate bit widths and node ranges at startup and reject illegal combinations, naming the offending key instead of silently defaulting.
feat.c8.desc: id() takes &mut self: the cross-thread sharing the PHP version warns about does not compile here. Share through Shared / Guard — no .await inside the lock.
feat.c9.desc: 89 tests (8-thread uniqueness, all three drift states, a fake Redis client), a reproducible benchmark, bilingual docs and the project mascot.
feat.footer: Requirements: Rust >= 1.88 (edition 2024) · any platform (i64) · one instance state per process; share across threads with Shared / Guard
life.title: ID Lifecycle
life.subtitle: The full path of one id() call, the instance state it keeps, and the capacity it is bounded by
life.bits.title: ID bit layout (64 bits by default)
life.bits.l1: The sign bit stays 0; the timestamp is a millisecond offset from the epoch
life.bits.l3: sequence 12 bits = 4096 IDs per millisecond (default layout)
life.state.title: Instance state (in memory, never shared across processes)
life.state.l1: last_timestamp — the millisecond of the previous ID; basis for drift and exhaustion checks
life.state.l2: resolver cursor — this millisecond's seq and last (each strategy keeps its own)
life.state.l3: epoch / fixed_bits — read-only after construction; &mut self blocks cross-thread sharing at compile time
life.state.note: For multiple threads use Shared / Guard: one state, one lock; build exactly one instance per (datacenter_id, worker_id)
life.cap.title: Capacity & throughput
life.cap.l1: At most 2^12 = 4096 IDs per millisecond; when exhausted, spin to the next millisecond and retry once.
life.cap.l2: That is 4.096M/s per node — generation measurably sits right at the sequence ceiling.
life.cap.l3: The default layout yields 32 × 32 = 1024 nodes; distribute (datacenter_id, worker_id) uniquely.
life.time.title: Lifespan timeline
life.time.l4: A more recent epoch resets the budget.
life.flow.n1.cap: Read the system clock as this call's time basis
life.flow.d1.cap: Yes → within clock_tolerance_ms the previous millisecond is reused; beyond it clock_drift_strategy decides: wait rides the drift out (within budget), throw raises ClockDrift.
life.flow.n2.cap: offset is the millisecond delta from the epoch
life.flow.d2.cap: Yes → a clock before the epoch raises ClockBeforeEpoch; an exhausted epoch raises TimestampOverflow.
life.flow.n3.cap: When the sequence is exhausted (None), spin to the next millisecond and retry once; still failing raises SequenceUnavailable, asking for a lower rate.
life.flow.n4.cap: State advances only after every guard passed: a failed call never poisons the next one.
